title: Customs Tariff Amendment (Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014
short_title: Customs Tariff Amendment (Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would change customs duties to put the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement into effect.
It would set zero duty rates for Korean goods that meet the origin rules in a new part of the Customs Act, adjust existing concessional rates, and phase some preferential rates down to zero by 2021.
A new schedule would list the preferential, phasing and excise-equivalent rates for alcohol, tobacco and petroleum products.
changes: Provides free rates of customs duty for Korean originating goods.
Amends Schedule 4 to maintain duty rates for certain Korean goods under concessional items.
Phases preferential rates for certain goods to Free by 2021.
Inserts a new Schedule 10 for preferential, phasing and excise-equivalent rates.
summary.affected: Importers of Korean originating goods and the Australian Customs and Border Protection Service.

speeches.speaker: Scott Morrison
speeches.brief: Introduced the Customs Amendment (Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014, which implements Australia's rules of origin obligations under the agreement, noting goods liberalisation alone is estimated to add nearly $5 billion to Australia's GDP between 2015 and 2030.

speeches.speaker: Scott Morrison
speeches.brief: Introduced the complementary Customs Tariff Amendment (Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014, which sets duty-free access and preferential tariff rates for Korean-originating goods, phasing these rates to zero by 2021.

speeches.speaker: Jim Chalmers
speeches.brief: Supported the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement bills as on balance in the national interest, citing forecasts of $3½ billion more in exports and 1,745 additional jobs by 2015, but moved an amendment urging the government to renegotiate the deal to remove investor-state dispute settlement provisions, protect labour market regulation and reverse automotive industry funding cuts.

speeches.speaker: Philip Ruddock
speeches.brief: Referred the Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills implementing the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement to the Federation Chamber for further consideration.

speeches.speaker: Laurie Ferguson
speeches.brief: Reported that the Human Rights Committee examined 12 bills, found nine required no further scrutiny, deferred one and identified two for further examination; it concluded that 10 of 12 matters concerning the Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (2014 Budget Measures No. 2) Bill 2014 were compatible with human rights.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Discussed the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement bill, noting the deal is expected to create about 1,700 jobs in its first year and boost the economy by $650 million after 15 years, while raising Labor's concerns about investor-state dispute settlement clauses that let corporations sue governments over policies harming their investments.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Questioned whether the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement served the national interest, citing its limited predicted GDP increase, concerns about investor-state dispute provisions, vehicle industry job losses, intellectual property, labour rights and access to 457 visas. Supported free trade agreements only where benefits extended beyond a small agricultural sector.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Robb
speeches.brief: Announced that the bill would amend the Customs Tariff Act 1995 to implement Australia's tariff commitments under the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement. Supported the agreement as opening markets, strengthening competitiveness and creating opportunities for exporters, workers, consumers and investors, and said it should deliver benefits once parliamentary procedures were completed.
